refined.title: Activation-Triggered Backdoor Detection via Outcome Indistinguishability
refined.summary: We propose detecting hidden backdoor triggers by testing outcome indistinguishability in model activations. The method identifies triggers by violating logical consistency in activation directions for perturbed inputs, evaluated on BackdoorBench and ELBA-Bench. The evaluation compares detection rates against STRIP and activation-clustering baselines, with ablations isolating the outcome indistinguishability mechanism.
refined.gap: BackdoorBench (ref-011) and ELBA-Bench (ref-013) show existing defenses (e.g., STRIP, ref-009) struggle against adaptive attacks. However, no method explicitly tests logical consistency in activation space for trigger detection, leaving open the question of whether outcome indistinguishability (ref-019) can identify stealthy triggers that evade current defenses.
refined.approach: Adapt ref-019's outcome indistinguishability to backdoor detection: for a model's activation space, identify directions where perturbed inputs (trigger + noise) violate logical consistency (e.g., a statement and its negation having opposite truth values). Inputs are perturbed by adding random patterns (as in STRIP, ref-009). A detector learns a direction in activation space that maximizes consistency violations, computed via linear probing without labeled data. The core difference from STRIP is using outcome indistinguishability (ref-019) instead of entropy-based classification.
refined.evaluation: Test on BackdoorBench (ref-011) using CIFAR-10 and GTSRB datasets with adaptive attacks (ref-011), and ELBA-Bench (ref-013) using 3 LLMs and 2 text datasets. Baselines include STRIP (ref-009) and activation clustering (ref-001). Metrics: true/false positive rates at a fixed threshold (FPR=1%). Ablation: compare outcome indistinguishability (ref-019) alone against STRIP's entropy-based detection on the same perturbed inputs.
